title: Passover night (Exodus 12:1–14)
hookLine: a lamb, blood on the doorposts, eaten in haste, and the angel passes over

cards: Some meals are just meals. Others get described for years afterward: who sat where, what was said, what the room smelled like. A last dinner before someone moved away.
The table the night before a wedding, or after a funeral. Exodus is about to describe a meal like that, the night before everything changes. Nine plagues have struck Egypt.
One more is coming, the death of the firstborn. And before it falls, God gives Moses and Aaron instructions. Not for a battle.

teach.b: Each household takes a lamb, a young male without blemish, and keeps it a few days.
At twilight, they kill it and put some of its blood on the two doorposts and the top of the door frame.

They roast it whole and eat it that night with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed for travel, in the King James Bible: "with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD's passover."
Shoes on, ready to walk out the door. Then the promise: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." That's the word: Pesach in Hebrew, Passover in English.
The plague will pass over the marked houses. And before any of it has happened, God says this night must be remembered: "this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast."
A feast of remembering, commanded before the event even begins. Jewish families still keep it.
At the Passover Seder, children ask why this night is different from all other nights, and the story is told again at the table. Christians carry this night too.
The Gospels set Jesus's last supper and his death at Passover time, and Paul writes, "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us."
That's why in many languages the word for Easter comes from Pesach: Pascha.

teach.h: WHEN I SEE THE BLOOD, I WILL PASS OVER YOU.
teach.b: The night carries grief too. The deliverance of one people came with death in the houses of another, and the Seder remembers that: a drop of wine is taken from the cup for each plague as it is named.

how: Jewish families keep Passover each spring with the Seder meal and the retelling of the Exodus; Christians celebrate Easter as their Pascha, and Catholic and other liturgical churches read Exodus 12 on Holy Thursday, the evening they remember the Last Supper.

s: God commanded Passover to be remembered before it happened
"this day shall be unto you for a memorial," said before the night began.

games.q: you're an Israelite father in Egypt. Moses says: kill a lamb, mark your doorposts with its blood, and eat it tonight dressed to travel. what do you do?
o: wait and see if the other families do it.
mark the door and eat in haste, shoes on.
games.why: the people do as they are told. "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." the night is to be remembered forever.

practice: Take a cracker, a piece of bread or a sip of water, and stand if you can, shoes on.
Eat slowly, as if you might have to leave, remembering a night that changed everything, for you or for someone who came before you and got out of something hard.
If you pray, you can give thanks for deliverance; if you don't, simply remember.

wordCard.voice: Passover. Pesach in Hebrew: the night the plague passed over the houses marked with the lamb's blood, kept as a feast of remembering ever since.

orig.note: Hebrew: Passover, from the verb to pass over or spare. the root of the Greek Pascha.

carryVoice: Your line: remember this night. Some nights are kept by being told again. Until tomorrow.
